So much fun! The food was delicious. The spare ribs were well seasoned and smoked just right. The dressing for the Smoked Chicken Cesar Salad was thick and yummy. Nice presentation for all the dishes. The staff was friendly. Two floors with a fantastic selections of multiplayer arcade games, like the 4-player Pac-Man, Super Chexx Bubble Hockey, Connect 4 Hoops, Air Hockey game table, 2-player Jurassic Park shooter arcade machine, to name a few. Just tap the pre-paid game card to start the game. There's also a photo booth that prints out 2 copies of photo set. Plenty of chairs, tables, and couches for enjoying drinks and hanging out on both floors. I was watching line dancing that was happening on the upper floor when I was outside. So cool!

Good:

Bad:

- Food is all pretty greasy and heavy

Overall this was a nice place to go with some friends but I wish it had more machines

Folks, let me tell you, Thriller is tremendous. It's a fantastic bar and arcade, believe me. The moment you walk in, you're hit with this incredible vibe – a perfect blend of retro and modern, just the best. The selection of arcade games is HUGE, really top-notch. They've got all the classics and the latest games, something for everyone. Tremendous!

Now, the bar – let me tell you, they make the best cocktails. I've had a lot of cocktails in my life, and these are some of the finest. Great variety, great flavors, just fantastic. The staff? Incredible. So friendly, so attentive, they really know how to take care of you.

The atmosphere is lively, but also very relaxed – it's the perfect balance. Clean, well-maintained, just beautifully done. And the themed nights and events? Absolutely fabulous. Always a great time, lots of fun, and you meet some amazing people.

Thriller is a winner, folks. If you want to have a great time, play some games, and enjoy some incredible drinks, this is the place. Highly, highly recommended. A+!

The staff is kind and happy to provide assistance. A fun outing in Oakland! #supportlocalbusinesses

What a cool concept! Definitely an interesting time, looking through all of the nostalgic shelves of computer games, but actually getting to play extremely niche games on the preserved systems was quite a treat. Plus you can leave and return on the same day, if you want to get a bite to eat in the downtown area, so it can be a full-day activity. All in all, completely worth the admission of $20.

The MADE is a really cool space with all sorts of games available to play, classes, and awesome volunteers! I recommend checking out the First Friday showcase, where local game developers come show off their indie games in development!

The place my 10yos want to go. Heck, I get sucked in to the retro and modern videogames here. Come for the classes and stay for the day; be warned that it's a fantastic destination for events so check their calendar frequently for scheduling interruptions

top_reviews.content:
Cute little theatre located in the heart of the Marina. They show a variety of films, including classics and new releases like some of the Oscar nominees for best picture. It's nice to have so many options for smaller independent movie theaters in San Francisco, so I try to support them.

This theatre is cozy, but it feels a bit old and tired. I was in cinema 2 and the sound felt muffled and the dialogue was sometimes difficult to understand. This was for a new release, so I don't think it was an issue with the film. I'm not sure if that's a common issue or not in this theatre.

The theatre wasn't too full on a Thursday evening. There were about a dozen other viewers.

Could be a nice spot for a date night, and there are lots of great restaurants nearby to eat at beforehand.
Since I’ve been going here, the issues with this theater have been more noticeable than before. Especially with the sound quality, grime, and outdated seating. It feels like a theater from the 90sz

They need to shut this place down. We waited 30 minutes for the movie to start and no one informed us about some problem in the projection booth. People had to go out and ask them to start the movie because they couldn’t be bothered to tell anyone waiting that there were issues. We just asked for a refund and left.

In a city brimming with excellent movie theaters, the Presidio is among my top choices! It's small but quaint, has fair prices for food & beverages, it has that classic old school cinema vibe, it's in a beautiful area of the city with some great shops & dining options nearby, and best of all, the theaters offer terrific viewing from virtually ever seat in the house. The slope per row is quite steep, meaning there likely won't be any heads blocking the screen from your view AND you won't strain your neck looking up at a screen for a couple hours - even the lower seats are lined up quite perfectly with the screen.

Tips: the movie started about 10 minutes after its scheduled starting time after a couple trailers meaning you have a bit of wiggle room if you are running late, and (at the time of writing this) tickets on online website such as Fandango are $15, but $14 at the door. There is no reserved seating, but perhaps if you're worried of the theater selling out, that extra dollar might be worth it.

The cutest neighborhood theater! Recently did a private screening here for my partner’s birthday and it was super fun- they even customized the marquee for us. Amazing experience and we’ll definitely find excuses to do it again in the future!

top_reviews.content: Beautiful simple and delightful cafe in Albany. Stopped for a Boba and Banh Mi and have fully made this one of my regular neighborhood spots. The sandwiches are killer. ❤️ And the owners are amazing. Definitely worth a stop!

When searching for a quick, easy, and filling lunch during my break, I ended up here at this cute little Viet Bagel & Banh Mi shop called Tay Tah Cafe!

When you first enter, you’re guided by arrows that lead you to the ordering tablet, or you can order at the main counter. The shop is small, but has plenty of counter seating and some small tables available as well! In between the front door and ordering, there’s a selection of chips and snacks for you to browse as well.

I was initially looking to order Banh Mi but was a bit intimidated by the $17/banh mi price tag. I opted in for an open face Asiago Bagel with Lox for $13 and placed my order. Breakfast orders that are $10+ get a free house coffee as well, so of course I opted in for it!

There’s a bathroom just around the corner from the ordering kiosk, but while I was making my way over there, the kind staff let me know that they are actually sold out of lox. They offered me a refund or to change what I ordered. I decided to switch to the Asiago Bagel with Ham, Bacon, Egg, and Cheese since it was the same price as the Lox!

My coffee came out first, and the person who gave me my coffee also filled up my cup with ice when I asked! The coffee itself had a nice deep & bitter flavor which I look for in a house coffee.

The sandwich was STUFFED full. I’ve never had a bagel breakfast sandwhich where I’ve quite had to unhinge my jaw like this. My photos did not do the sandwich justice, but I promise it’s so much bigger than you’d expect!

The eggs were perfectly fluffy and smothered in cheese. The ham and bacon were cooked to my personal liking. If you like crispy bacon, maybe mention that to them, because it was perfectly chewy for me. The bagel, was soft, fluffy, yet so bouncy, and I LOVE that there are poppy seeds mixed into their Asiago bagel.

The cost to quantity ratio for the breakfast sandwich was 100% worth it. I’ll definitely be back when I need a hearty sandwich.

top_reviews.content: Wow. I think I found my favorite coffee shop in Oakland.  It’s quite lovely with its beautiful shiny tiled green panel. After tasting them, I went in to ask for a bit more of the specialty syrups that come with those drinks. Instead, the staff pictured told me four times to go add simple syrup myself which isn’t the same thing. The looks and tone I received felt very condescending and dismissive. We paid $15 plus a tip; I don’t think asking for more of the syrup that’s already part of the drink is an unreasonable request.

The latte is good and is more on the light roast side (which seems to be their preference here). They also host classes. The inside is really nice but the seating is a bit difficult for coworking. They do have tables outside and an outdoor area!

We recently visited a charming coffee house in Oakland, known for its specialty in pour-over coffee. When we arrived in the morning, the place wasn't too busy, and we were pleased to find plenty of comfortable seating areas. The coffee shop offers a variety of coffee beans sourced from different parts of the world, and they even have their own coffee roasting and tasting room. This was the first coffee shop I've ever visited with a coffee brewing lab, which was quite impressive.

We ordered a filtered pour-over (Colombia Edwin Norena), a latte, and an iced coffee, along with two pastries. The pastries were delicious, and the coffees were flavorful, although not overly strong. The pour-over coffee, in particular, stood out for its lack of bitterness. I also noticed another customer ordering an espresso flight, which was presented beautifully. I look forward to trying that next time.

I absolutely love this place! The atmosphere is fantastic—cozy and inviting—though seating is quite limited, especially in the mornings when it gets busy. They have a special Tasting Room that offers stellar coffee service, with diverse counter heights perfect for drinks and light bites. The space also features an impressive 8-tap system and a mobile modular coffee bar called “Naaga,” crafted by Oakland artist Chambers Art & Design.

The aroma of fresh coffee here is incredible. Today, I ordered a 4oz espresso with milk made from the Kenya Kii Peaberry Washed beans, as well as a menu item called Leila by Alisha Rajan. The Leila is mischievous and magical—a sparkling iced Americano with fig and ginger syrup, topped with ume plum coconut whipped cream and garnished with candied ginger. It’s like Leila, the black cat, inviting you to play along. The Leila uses Tanzanian beans and, although the portions are small and prices on the higher side, the quality is absolutely worth it. The coffee is fragrant and intensely flavorful.

If you enjoy fruity coffee blends, Leila is a must-try. The staff explain the coffees in a way that’s easy to understand and really enhances the experience. I’ll definitely be coming back—just wish there were more seats! Parking is street-side with a coin meter, so plan accordingly.

For snacks, we tried an aloo tikki roll wrapped in paratha. It was decent but nothing particularly memorable. The paratha was a bit too oily and greasy, and overall, it felt slightly overpriced for the portion size. We also tried another pastry with a mango cream cheese filling, which was okay but not outstanding.

Overall, I really enjoyed the authentic chai and cozy atmosphere. While some of the snacks were hit or miss, the tea and desserts made the visit worthwhile. If you’re a fan of real Indian chai, this place is definitely worth a stop.

top_reviews.content:

On New Years Eve 2025, exactly one year ago, I was assaulted outside of the Vogue Theater.

I had a rough 2024. Lost my job, Got out of a relationship. Lost my car. Was dealing with the loss of my cat. Ended up cutting myself off and lost friendships. It does not necessarily justify it, but it comes as no surprise that on 12/31/24, I was desperately trying to self medicate. I had gone to the Vogue Theater for a Purple Rain/ Sign ‘O’ The Times double feature. I had been drinking prior to going to the movie theater, and ordered another beer when I arrived. After the countdown, I continued to get drunk off prepoured champagne glasses. At one point, I remember grabbing the entire champagne bottle and stowing away in the bathroom. I am not trying to make excuses for or defend my actions, but at the time, these actions made sense as a coping mechanism. Eventually I was confronted by the owners of the theater, taken outside and asked to leave. I distinctly remember one of the owners bragging about how he knew the local cops and he could ring them right then and now. And for whatever reason, despite the fact that they were two grown men dealing with one drunk unarmed individual who posed ZERO physical threat, they pepper sprayed me at point blank range. Regardless of how much I'd drank, this is absolutely not how you should act as an event host, especially at an NYE party. At no point was I asked if I was okay, nor was I offered water.

After walking from the theater with absolutely no sense of direction, I remember passing out at a bus stop. freezing and no idea how to get home. At some point around 4am, I woke up and saw a driver pull up and offer me a ride claiming to be an Uber driver. Now, normally, one would be more skeptical, but that was proven difficult after I had been pepper sprayed and chased out. I distinctly remember while sitting in the passenger seat, the driver groping my thigh, telling me to stay still. Despite the pepper spray, despite all the drinks, I remember feeling completely paralyzed as the streets started to take shape. I remember yelling at the top of my lungs and screaming my address. When we finally arrived, the driver paused, and then noticed that my roommate was coming home right at that same time as well. If that coincidence hadn't occurred, I have no idea how worse that night could have gone.

I spent New Years Day 2025 in bed, nursing a hangover and a remarkably swollen and burnt face, and put Heat and Moonstruck on the TV. I knew I needed to make a change. Despite the fact that my face still burned and would continue to burn for the next week, I went back to the Vogue Theater to retrieve a hat I'd left near my seat. After giving me back my hat and reprimanding me once more, the same man from the night laughed and asked me “how'd you like that face full of pepper spray?” Tomorrow, New Years Day 2026, will mark one year sober for me. I am very happy to have made this milestone, am incredibly appreciative of the support my friends and family have extended, and above all, am grateful for the clarity and confidence it's given me to speak up about how terribly I was treated by the staff at the Vogue Theater last year, who were too bent on playing cowboy than they were helping a patron.

top_reviews.content: I love that you can bring your own food and drinks ($5 charge per person for alcohol). I had the Daft Punk room for 8 people. The folks that check you in are friendly and great customer service. The song selection was great with variety of languages, genres, artists and eras, sound system was good. With the space and bodies in there it can get toasty with the singing, dancing, and drinking. I run very warm so at one point had to step out to get air. This was my first time here and we were celebrating the holidays and the start of a 2 week work break. I am definitely coming back.

I’ve been coming to Fillmore Karaoke for around 15 years now, and it’s been great to see how the system has been updated over the years. They have a really good song selection—we usually sing English, Mandopop, and Cantopop—and they’ve had most of the songs we’ve wanted.

The current system is very easy to use and has some features that I don’t always see at other karaoke places:

* Easily browse top songs of all time or search by artist or song name
* Shuffle songs
* Fast-forward through songs, which is great for songs with long intros
* Add or remove the singer’s voice

We also tried scanning the QR code to use our phones as a remote, but it didn’t work for us. We just took turns sitting near the screen to manage the songs instead.

The song selection is pretty extensive, although we did run into a few songs that showed “Downloading” after selecting them but never actually downloaded. I’d recommend checking that the song was successfully added to the queue before assuming it’s there.

The rooms are clean and spacious, as they have always been in my experience, and we’ve never had an issue with them. If you come during happy hour, rooms are 35% off before 8 p.m., which is a great deal.

A few things to know before you go:

* The front desk will ask how long you plan to use the room. If there are other guests waiting or a reservation after yours, that will determine your end time.
* There is a minimum one-hour charge. After the first hour, you’re charged in 15-minute increments if you don’t use a full additional hour.
* They aren’t always very clear about the exact timing, so I’d recommend noting your start time and setting your own timer so you know when your room time is ending.
* There is a credit card processing fee as well as an additional mandatory fee.

Overall, this has been one of my go-to karaoke spots for years. The rooms are consistently clean and spacious, the song selection is great, and I really like how easy the current system is to use. Just keep an eye on your timing and the extra fees when booking.

top_reviews.content: I visited Bella Cafe recently and had a genuinely lovely experience. I was at the register asking if the hot chocolate was made with real cacao like the ones in Europe and while the cashier said they make it with Ghirardheli powder, a man interrupted our conversation to say, “ We are not hiring. “ I was being amicable and was smiling and froze since never in my life have I faced this level of stereotyping or discrimination. I didn’t answer back because I never mistreat people at service. I know my privilege. But it turns out the person who spoke to me was THE Italian OWNER. I was flabbergasted and very uncomfortable but truly I didn’t know what to do. I later told the waiter how wrong of a thing to say to a customer that was. He replied it was a joke. I told him, “it’s wrong to discriminate, you are in California.”
Ultimately, im never coming back to this new place. Fidi is my home being beside Nobhill and this interaction by an OWNER is just unacceptable. Terrible values. I don’t want to go to places that are selectively polite, since when I left he was being very talkative to ppl outside. I have been going all these years to ONE65 and everyone is so outstanding ALWAYS and the pastries look sooo much better. From the greeting at the door to other points of contact with the customer.

This was very unprofessional.

top_reviews.content: One of the best coffee shops in the Bay. Great espresso drinks, top quality drip coffee, and love the assortment of Mexican and/or locally inspired food and products. I ordered the dirty chai latte with oat milk paired with a raspberry jam-filled treat, and the combination was incredible.The espresso in the dirty chai added a great bold kick that balanced out the warming chai spices. Choosing oat milk was definitely the right call—it made the drink super creamy and gave it a smooth, velvety texture without being overly heavy.The real magic happened when pairing it with the pastry. The bright, tart sweetness of the raspberry jam cut right through the rich, spicy notes of the latte. It kept the whole experience from feeling too sugary or overwhelming.Highly recommend this exact combo if you want something comforting with a great balance of sweet, tart, and spicy flavors. Will absolutely be back for this exact order!

This is one of West Oakland’s favorites, and to be fair, is quite hidden from the naked eye — unless you decide to explore the area in more detail. This coffee shop is honestly unique in its own way — the Western kick of coffee meets the Mexican style of pan, tamales, and more.

Upon going there many times, i find that they have a wide variety of things that none other coffee shop can do better: horchata lattes. To my surprise they’re honestly one of the best in the area. They source their coffee beans locally from Oakland and Hayward, and their syrups are made from scratch. In addition, they get their tamales from a local tamal factory in Hayward — which tastes authentic and of region.

They also give really good hospitality, and the design of the coffee shop is very modern and chique. I will say the down side of this coffee shop is that they have limited seating inside, and the outside seating is usually pretty cold, so some people just take their food & drinks to go. Otherwise, I’d recommend this place forsure!

top_reviews.content:
Great Venue for electronic music. Ample room to find your spot to dance or socialize. Sound system is loud so bring some ear plugs!

I’m writing this review because I genuinely want to see this venue and its events do better — especially since the concept for this night was excellent on paper.

I attended “Desmadre: Bachata vs. Cumbia” on 1/31/26, specifically because the event title and promotion clearly suggested a night centered on bachata and cumbia. That was the sole reason my friends and I bought tickets. Unfortunately, the event was not at all what was advertised.

When we arrived, the music being played was general Latin/club music, but neither bachata nor cumbia. We asked other attendees whether those genres had been played earlier, and they said only briefly, if at all. Later, after speaking directly with the DJ and staff, I learned that the DJ only plays vinyl — and that bachata “basically doesn’t exist on vinyl,” which explained why no bachata was played at all during the night.

That raises a serious issue. If an event is marketed around specific genres:

- the DJ should be able to deliver those genres, or

- the event name and promotion should be changed to reflect reality, or

- an exception should be made (digital/CDs/etc.) to honor what was promised to ticket buyers.

None of those things happened here.

Eventually, some cumbia was played, but it was short-lived, and there was no bachata at all. For dancers like me — who don’t dance salsa and were excited to finally attend an event where we wouldn’t have to sit songs out — this was deeply disappointing. Had we known what the music would actually be, we would not have purchased tickets.

This isn’t about taste or preference; it’s about accurate advertising and respect for your audience. A great concept fell flat because execution didn’t match promotion.

I hope the organizers take this feedback seriously, because the idea behind this event was solid — it just wasn’t delivered as promised.

top_reviews.content:
I recently attended an event at Lions Den Bar and Lounge in Chinatown with a large group from my organization. The experience was a mixed bag for me, but here’s a breakdown:

Food:
I tried the wings, spring rolls, and chow mein, and all were seasoned pretty well. I’m not sure if the food was made in-house or catered, but it was decent overall. I also had a couple of drinks—Stella and a Gin and Tonic—which were standard but good.

Service:
The staff seemed fine, though I didn’t have much interaction with them beyond ordering drinks. Payment options were a bit limited, as I didn’t notice tap-to-pay, and most people just used their cards.

Ambience:
This is where things were a little hit-or-miss for me. When we arrived around 5:00pm, the place was pretty empty, but it picked up when our event started at 6:00pm. The seating was adequate, though some people in our group had to stand, but it didn’t seem to bother them. The lighting was actually a highlight, with colorful lights adding a nice vibe as the evening went on.

The real fun began when karaoke started—definitely a high point! It really lifted the mood, especially since the Padres vs Dodgers game was also on the screens, adding to the entertainment.

Overall:
If you’re looking for a spot for a group event, this place might do the trick, especially with the added fun of karaoke and a game on TV. However, if I were going solo or with just one other person, I’d probably choose another spot, as the overall vibe just wasn’t for me.

Came here for dinner, first time visiting this place even though I've passed by many times since it opened.  The place was busy, but there were still a good amount of tables to sit in.  I think we only waited a minute, and the waitress sat us down and got us tea all within a couple of minutes.  The decoration and atmosphere is casual with a sense that you are in a Hong Kong style restaurant with a large mural of a Hong Kong street with lots of store front signs and neon lights.  The decoration is eclectic with an Asian theme with lots of little Asian themed toys and knickknacks.

The food menu is extensive with lots of common foods found in street cafes such as toasts, baked rice, and noodles dishes to the more common dishes like fried rice, Chow mien, porridge, etc. Then there is the more oddball and exotic dishes made with intestines, blood, and frogs.

As I wasn't into experimenting into the exotic dishes we decided to order BBQ pork fried rice,  salt & pepper deep fried fish, salt & pepper deep fried tofu, wonton soup, western style overeasy egg in minced beef sauce over rice, and stir-fry beef rib-eye Japan style.

All the dishes came in within the next 10 to 15 minutes.  They looked delicious to my eyes and smelled even better.   The bbq pork unfortunately did not meet my satisfaction.  Yeah, it looked great and smelled good, but the taste was just bland.  There wasn't even a taste of the bbq pork. The pork itself was dry, like the remnants of old bbq pork cuttings that have been sitting for a while.  Fortunately the other dishes were arriving and we had a better experience.

The next dish to come was the wonton soup. The bowl had enough soup and wonton dumplings to serve at least all four of us with a couple extras.  There were also fresh baby bok Choi vegetables in the soup, which was nice to balance all the meat.  The soup was okay,  nothing exciting.  The meat filling in the wonton was okay too... I've had better.

The next dish up was the salt & pepper tofu cubes. These deep-fried morsels were piping hot with a nice outer crunch and very soft interior.  The outside had a really nice seasoning that was savory with a hint of spices. There were also sprinkling of fried jalapeño peppers and garlic.  It was delicious.

The next dish was the salt & pepper deep fried fish.  Just like the tofu,  these fish were battered and deep fried and seasoned with salt, spices,  and that mixture of jalapeños pepper and fried garlic. The fish was delicious with a semi crunchy outer shell and a very nice soft, smooth, almost melty interior. I'm not sure what type of fish they used, but it was really nice and soft.

A minute later, the waitress brought out the rest of our order.  It was the overeasy egg in minced beef and sauce over rice and the stir-fry beef rib-eye Japan style.

The western style egg in minced beef sauce over rice was truly delicious.  It was a mound of rice with a brown gravy sauce with minced beef and shavings of I think it was broccoli stems. In the middle of all that mess was a raw egg cooking in the heat of the dish.  The beef and sauce mixed in with the rice was just great.  I really can't explain the taste, it was like putting gravy into your rice but the gravy is not over powering. It balanced the right amount of saltiness, beef flavor, and umami to go right with the plain white rice.

My favorite dish above all the stir-fry beef ribeye Japan style dish.  The pieces of beef are stir fried in a sweet, savory sauce with a very distinctive flavor I couldn't identify.  Under the beef are pan fried soft tofu rounds that have the sauce dripping on it.  Surrounding the beef and tofu is a bed of fresh broccoli with drippings of sauce on top.  This dish was really exceptionally good.  The beef was so tender and juicy with the addition of the sauce that it was an explosion of flavor and texture in your mouth.

We truly ate really well and had lots of leftover for the next day.  I'll probably visit again and try their other dishes.  Some of the dishes you can't find in regular Chinese restaurants.

The vibe here is truly authentic. With its open, airy layout and floods of natural light, it captures that specific "Grand Café" energy found in Europe’s great capitals. It’s the kind of place where you can linger over a perfect espresso and actually feel the pulse of the city without the usual rush.

Why it works:

Versatility: Whether you need fast Wi-Fi for studying, a chic spot for a quick lunch, or a place to catch up with friends, there is tons of seating to accommodate.

The Bakery: The selection is a visual and culinary treat—definitely don't skip the pastries!

The Location: It’s perfectly situated for a post-coffee stroll down to City Hall park to take in the views.

This cafe is more than just a business; it’s a beautiful sign of the renewal of SF downtown. It brings a sophisticated, European-style community hub to the neighborhood that we’ve been missing. I could not recommend it more!

My go to breakfast items are the Spinach Feta Empanadas and the Date Latte. P.S. the music adds a nice touch to the place.

Bench holds such a special place in our hearts and in our community! It is our favorite spot to enjoy a delectable, freshly baked pastry, cake, cookie, or scone along with a coffee drink or matcha latte prepared just perfectly. The aesthetic is perfect — welcoming, light, bright, airy, with touches of greenery and color. The music always sets a lovely backdrop too. And most importantly, the owner Sanaz and her husband, along with all of the incredible baristas including Norah, create an utterly wonderful vibe for the café. The space promotes productive work both downstairs and above the spiral staircase, but also conversations and connections in a welcoming community setting. From the Persian cookies to the unbelievably soft fall-apart blueberry scones, the food is only matched by the cheerful and warm atmosphere that permeates Bench. It is always so fun to see what the baked goods will be — it’s like a delicious little surprise (unless one takes a peak on IG where they are sometimes revealed ahead of time, hehe)!

Thank you Sanaz and team for an incredible community space. We absolutely love coming to Bench and leave this review in order to share with others the cozy little gem on MLK Way that has a cozy little spot in our hearts! ❤️

I am only docking off a point because Signal could definitely hire more people. The one barista on shift at the moment, was truly knocking out the long lines forming.

Will I go to a Berkeley rep show again? … prob…
to see a musical…

Directing, lighting, acting, overall cleverness, realism of script

Great Notion Brewery: Berkeley's Explosion of Flavor and Innovation

Our insatiable thirst for exciting breweries and unique beers led us to Great Notion Brewery in Berkeley, and let me tell you, it was a revelation. Great Notion truly lives up to its name. Their beers are unlike anything you've ever experienced – bursting with flavor, pushing boundaries, and offering something truly special for every taste bud.

Convenience and Comfort: A Smooth Start to Your Adventure

Finding parking in Berkeley can sometimes be a hassle, but Great Notion makes things easy. They offer decent street parking options, and for those who prefer a contactless experience, pay-by-phone parking is readily available. Once you've secured your spot, head inside for a comfortable and relaxing atmosphere. The seating is described as "decent," suggesting a good mix of tables and chairs to accommodate groups of all sizes.

The MVP Hall of Fame: Electric Headband, Over Ripe Fruit, and More!

Now, let's dive into the main event – the incredible beers!  Great Notion boasts a wide range of styles, but your review highlights a few true champions:

Electric Headband (MVP): I can  describe this beer as "to die for" with its vibrant blue color and surprising blue raspberry flavor. A beer this unique deserves a visit on its own!

Over Ripe Fruit in the Can (MVP): This "mango heaven" sounds like a smoothie lover's dream come true. It's a testament to Great Notion's innovative spirit and their ability to create truly delicious and unexpected flavor combinations.

Munchies: This imperial stout takes the cake for intriguing ingredients. Combining pretzels, potato chips, and peanut butter might seem strange on paper, but a "complex" and "soulful" taste hints at a truly unique and satisfying experience.

GR 75: This red tart ale sounds like a delightful burst of tropical fruit flavors. I can mention notes of guava and raspberry, making it a perfect choice for those who enjoy a refreshing and slightly sour brew.

RIPE: As an IPA lover, my declaration that this is "one of the best IPAs I've ever tasted" is high praise indeed. It suggests a perfectly balanced and flavorful IPA that will leave any hop-head happy.

A Must-Visit for Beer Adventurers and Traditionalists Alike

Great Notion Brewery caters to all palates. Whether you're a seasoned craft beer enthusiast seeking the next boundary-pushing brew, or a casual drinker looking for something unique and delicious, Great Notion has something for you. They even offer non-alcoholic options, like the "Black Cherry Cream Soda" – creamy, different, and perfect for those who want to enjoy the experience without the alcohol.

This place is a true gem, and with so many incredible beers on tap (including the "Beer Has No Name" hazy IPA), it's no surprise id plan to return for more.

top_reviews.content: So, my friend and I visited this museum for shits and giggles, but honestly, we were not disappointed. This place had one room full of displays and information on the history of the creation of the vibrator, its origins, and its development throughout the centuries. It was clean, organized, and easy to interact with some of the displays. Plus, it's free and open to the public during store hours, so why not? It's a nice little bonus to the adult shop here, and I give the place two thumbs up!

Great experience at the whole location. The museum was a large room at the back of the store that told the history well. Loved having educators running the shop so questions were easy to ask and I was comfortable the whole time. Worth the stop.

2024 EDIT AT END.

Very informative and fun and wild at times. It's a small room in the back of the store, so more of an exhibit than a museum. 20-30 minutes to fully look at everything. Should probably call ahead because it seems like the hours can sometimes be weird.

In order to visit the museum, you need a photo ID (not sure what the age restriction was, though) and you need to be comfortable walking through a store full of sex toys and related merchandise, but if you're thinking of visiting the Antique Vibrator Store, you're probably already there.

EDIT: I've been meaning to edit this for months since I learned that the narrative from Rachel Maines that the museum supports is actually a myth. A lot of the history in the museum is still legit and the vibrators in the museum are certainly real and still very cool, but I hope that the museum provides more clarity on this point (rating switched from 5 to 3 stars for now). As another sex historian Hallie Lieberman notes in a 2020 article for the NY Times,

"The myth can be traced to Rachel Maines’s 1999 book “Technology of Orgasm” (she wrote some earlier articles, but the book is what put this version of the vibrator’s history on the map). Published by Johns Hopkins University Press, “Technology” seemed like a well-researched scholarly book, with 465 citations and a plethora of primary sources, some in Greek and Latin; the problem is that none of them actually supported this story. (Ms. Maines has said she put forth her version as an “interesting hypothesis” and never intended it to be seen as established fact.) Nonetheless, the idea caught on and spread."

Here's a citation for the scholarly article Liberman co-wrote to debunk the myth:

Lieberman, Hallie and Eric Schatzberg, "A Failure of Academic Quality Control: The Technology of
Orgasm." Journal of Positive Sexuality 4, no. 2 (2018): 24-47.

EDIT 2: Sadly we're down to 2 stars till hopefully it's updated. Upon finally editing this review I read the entire academic article from the Journal of Positive Sexuality mentioned above, and it turns out that a lot more of the historical timeline in the museum (which I have pictures of from a year ago) are misleading in the same way that Rachel Maines's use of those "sources" were misleading (the article touches on Galen, Forestus, Highmore, and Taylor). The museum's founder (Joani Blank) is even referenced in the article for her partial critique of the myth.

More importantly, I thought that the account in the academic article about how easily Maines's book was accepted and used in academics, law, and pop culture (not to mention vibrator museums), is far more interesting than the false narrative Maines put forth. I would readily watch that movie over the various films made about this vibrational myth.

I have passed by here so many times on my way to other places, and I finally decided to try it because lately I’ve been visiting places that don’t have a lot of heavy promotion or gimmicks.

The price may seem steep to some people, but I was born and raised and in the east bay so I can understand how hard it is to keep a business to stay here so I don’t mind. Besides— the actual price you pay is for the kind service and food that is made with love.

I was raised by my grandparents and the feeling I get when I’m at Nina’s cafe makes me feel like they’re still alive and taking care of me like they used to do. You can tell she prepares everything she makes with love and it’s something she’s passionate about.

I will keep returning!

The last time I went was on a Tuesday and it was pretty low key, but perfect for the vibe we were looking for. The food was good and I even enjoyed their signature mocktail. Last, but not least, customer service is A1! All the staff are friendly, fun, and accommodating.

My friend & I have been searching for another sports bar to check out in Oakland; one that'll cover basketball & soccer in particular. There are very few bars we know of that show soccer games, but we decided to take a chance and made a reservation at Mushin to watch the El Clásico. Here is a summary of our experience today:

Ambiance - clean, classy, and feels like a party all at once with the DJ playing music in the background (mixture of 90s-00s hip-hop/R&B). The back area was reserved for a private party, which can be organized separately with staff for future social events. Plenty of TV screens throughout. It was pretty busy when we arrived at 12:45pm on a Sunday, so we were grateful for making the reservation ahead of time.

Drinks - signature cocktails were distinct from each other & delicious. I had the caipirinha & Tap Tap cocktails (only one of which I could show, because the other I lovingly consumed right away), whereas my friend had a few IPAs. Prices are standard Bay Area-wise ($5-6 for beers, $10-15 for cocktails)

Food - good, but limited. They do have a brunch menu which is separate from another I've seen online. Fried chicken & waffles were nice. If you're extremely hungry, I'd recommend eating elsewhere beforehand, as portions are small-medium at best.

Service -  the staff were very amicable and willing to accommodate our needs, whether it be changing the channels to our requested game, making friendly banter, or checking in on us to make sure everything was met despite how busy it was.

Overall, our time here was fantastic! Needless to say, I will be coming back here again and bringing along other friends to share the same experience. But also because I'm awfully curious about this avocado margarita... Cheers!

The Marsh is a community performing arts theater in Downtown Berkeley with two areas - a 75-120 seat main area for plays, as well as a secondary 60 seat cabaret area with bar. The plays (often by solo performers) are high quality and reasonably priced, and there are occasionally free shows for the public.

In addition to being a performance space, the Marsh also hosts community classes for children and adults. Some of these local and up-and-coming performers can be seen in the recurring weekly and monthly events, both in Berkeley and SF.

top_reviews.content:
If you're in Oakland or the San Francisco area, you absolutely must visit this incredible gem! The experience is genuinely authentic and refreshingly unfiltered. Jill, the host, has transformed the lower level of her home into a museum that pays homage to the Black Panther movement, allowing visitors to explore its history and the various programs created to uplift communities.

She has preserved original newspapers from the Black Panther era, creating a rich educational atmosphere. Jill is friendly, knowledgeable, and deeply passionate about sharing the positive impact of the Black Panthers on both local and global communities.

I discovered this treasure by chance, not realizing that it was her home upstairs and a museum downstairs, so I recommend scheduling an appointment to ensure you receive a proper tour. It’s conveniently located just 2 blocks away from the Black Panthers' national 4th headquarters and 1 block away a statue of Huey P. Newton, along with numerous murals outside of Jill’s home and throughout the area.

I'm so glad I had the opportunity to visit. I encourage everyone to experience this museum and consider donating to support Jill’s efforts in continuing to educate others about this significant movement. It's truly a must-see!

Coming here with my educator union after visiting Black Joy Parade. The Women Black Panther Museum was very empowering to visit.

We got a stellar tour the owner Jill whom bought it in 2000. She informed us that she had it to empower her self and the community of shining the light on Black Women that shine their light in their communities and are role models.

This is her way of resistance and made it with the context to ensure everyone in the neighborhood is acknowledged by saying hi to them. This was very uplifting as no one is erased.

I really appreciated the tour and was surprised to see the Turkeys 🦃 roaming freely! And a walk away is the Huey Statue.

Thanks for having us Jill!

If you're in Oakland or the San Francisco area, you absolutely need to visit this gem! The experience is incredibly authentic and far from whitewashed. The host has preserved original newspapers from the Black Panther era, creating a rich educational atmosphere. She is friendly, knowledgeable, and truly passionate about sharing the history and positive impact of the Black Panthers on the community and beyond. If you have the chance, please check it out, and consider donating to support her efforts in continuing to educate others about this important movement. It's a must-see!

Enlightening and inspiring. A must see on any visit to Oakland. Reading an article in a 1970s BPP newspaper by Mumia Abu Janal when he was still a free and a journalist was invigorating. YET, the focus on the women of the BPP even more uplifting. Hail to the women of the BPP. ALL POWER TO THE PEOPLE!

Jill is the owner of the house and has graciously allowed the first floor of her home to be dedicated to sharing info about the Black Panther Party. I think she prefers you make an appointment, but she does have hours and instructions on the door for drop-ins. There is a $12'p/person donation she collects at the end of your self-guided tour. You must take off your shoes or use the shoe covers she provides to enter. She'll give you a brief introduction of the layout, then leave you to explore on your own. She also has merchandise (magnets, posters, stickers, shirts) you can purchase. Beyond the museum experience, she was very helpful to our group by providing other sites to see in the neighborhood and to recommend other experiences in Oakland.
I'm so glad the staff at Marcus Books recommended we go there.

Well, what can I say about this place?

The Black Panther Party Museum, Oakland

As someone who went to Merritt College, I had learned about the history of the Black Panther Party from there. Merritt College has many photos and historical documents there that I wanted to learn more about it.

The Black Panther Party was founded in 1966 by Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale. They met at Merritt College in Oakland. The movement started out small in Oakland’s Black communities, starting with feeding young children to opening up clinics for people of all ages.

Huey also went to China and met with many politicians and famous people there, the black and yellow community united together and not a lot of history mentions that.

This museum is located in Downtown Oakland, it is pretty small and has another room dedicated to Oscar Grant as well. The museum is free but accepts donations. The staffs were friendly and greets you when you walk in.

Would go again if I’m in the area.

The Oakland Museum has a small area about the Black Panther party as well, but it’s paid admission.

I visited the Black Panther Museum in Oakland today and left with a much deeper understanding of this pivotal movement in American history. Located in the heart of the city where the Black Panthers were founded, the museum does an excellent job of presenting the Party’s full story, not just the imagery most people know, but their community programs, like a complimentary breakfast for children, health clinics, and education initiatives. The exhibits are thoughtfully curated, featuring original photographs, newspaper clippings, and personal artifacts that bring the 1960s and 70s to life. What struck me most was how the museum humanizes the Panthers’ members, showing them as organizers and activists working to address real problems in their communities: poverty, police brutality, and lack of access to basic services. The staff are knowledgeable and passionate, happy to answer questions and provide context. Whether you’re familiar with this history or just learning about it, the museum offers a valuable perspective on a movement that shaped Oakland and influenced social justice efforts nationwide. It’s a small space but packed with powerful stories that deserve to be told. Highly recommend for anyone interested in civil rights history or in better understanding Oakland’s legacy of activism.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

The Cube is such an exciting addition to SF's art scene! Opened October 25, 2024, this is the new home of the San Francisco Art Institute, relocated from their previous location to this stunning five-story modernist building at 345 Montgomery Street. The exhibition space has more than doubled from 11,000 to 26,000 square feet, and the transformation is incredible.

The building itself is a work of art - originally the flagship Bank of America branch from 1971, redesigned by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill with a dramatic five-story atrium featuring grand staircases and cantilevered walkways. Located right at the corner of California and Montgomery Streets in the heart of the Financial District, it's super accessible by public transit.

What I love most is that admission is completely free! They focus on experimental contemporary art exhibitions that rotate regularly, often addressing social and cultural issues. No permanent collection, which keeps things fresh and dynamic. They also offer free workshops on weekends which is a nice touch.

Open Wednesday-Sunday 11am-5pm, with extended Thursday hours until 7pm. I'd recommend visiting Thursday evenings when it's less crowded. Perfect to combine with other nearby art venues like SFMOMA for a full art day. This transformation of a vacant bank into vibrant cultural space really represents downtown SF's renaissance!

Super excited to visit this museum. We all came from different parts of the city using public transportation and it was super easy to get to. It blends in and easy to miss as it’s tucked in the corner at the bottom of the BofA building at the corner of Montgomery. The displays are on 2 floors. They have a makers section so great of you have budding little ones who want to create something. Best of all…it’s free!

I am so grateful we have places like ICA SF in San Francisco. Art is extremely important in today’s society, where technology is overpowering creativity and empathy and understanding is becoming increasingly rare. Art is a universal tool for learning; about other perspectives, about history, and just about humanity in general, which is why I’m so glad that ICA SF makes it free and accessible to all.

The building occupied by ICA SF is just as beautiful as the art held within it, which is fitting. It shares the block with another wonderful building, 555 California Street, and is attached to the concourse. All of the art on display when I visited was impressive and moved me in one way or another. I liked that the spaces around the pieces correlated with the art displayed, that’s something I don’t see a lot in other art museums. My favorite exhibit of the three I saw had to be the Midnight March exhibit. Mainly because the figures were cute, but also because it was based off of a Japanese folktale. As an Asian, it’s always inspiring to see art surrounding Asian experiences and history, and I think we need more of it. There was also an area near the back where visitors could make art, and I had a great time creating as well as seeing others’ creations. There were also areas to read books, and restrooms.

The only reason I give ICA SF 4 stars is because I think it could use more art! I know that free admission is already very generous, but there were empty spots here and there which I thought could totally use a display. I also think ICA SF could have more potential if the upper three floors were used, but I’m guessing there is some kind of barrier to that. Lastly, there are occasional clanking sounds coming through the walls of the building due to it being next to the underground parking garage, but that is a minor issue that can’t really be fixed.

Overall, I’m so happy I stumbled across this place. 4/5.

That thing is big enough to split, no lie.
It’s less of a dessert and more of an event,
The kind you order once and then feel financially spent.
They’ve even got cookie dough scoops on the side,
For people who want to skip the shake ride.
Just straight-up dough in its own little section,
Which is either dangerous or a great invention.
The flavors rotate, so it stays pretty fresh,
Seasonal options slide in with the rest.
So even if you’ve gone once, there’s still a reason

Or talk to someone up front and do the human pick.

TLDR:
Overall: Fun, extremely sweet (although pricy) over-the-top milkshakes
My Order: Brookie Batter Specialty Milkshake
Price Breakdown: $23.90 (including tax, etc for a pricier one of the milkshake options)

So this was one insane milkshake. After seeing pictures online of these over-the-top fantasy-esque milkshakes and realized there was a new location in Berkeley, I was very intrigued and finally made my way down. We got the specialty milkshake (mostly bc it comes with the souvenir glass that they let you clean and take home after) and I promise you this is enough for two people for sure. There were a lot of moving parts in our Brookie Batter Specialy Millshake, cookie dough icecream, a brownie, a cookie, lots of chocolate chips, a definitely very pretty dessert.

This was a very sweet dessert (almost needed to wash down with water at some point) and we were incredibly full by the end of it, even when we shared it. The flavors were very fun at first, but as we continued, it did get a bit overwhelming and the tastes merged together a bit. The milkshake part ended up being a bit more refreshing than the rest of it. And unfortunately but understandably the price is quite a bit steep for the milkshake, but this was a very complex treat with lots of different components that made it a bit more worth it. The staff was also lovely and helpful in getting utensils and choosing a milkshake.

Overall, definitely not trying to be a regular here (for the sake of my health 😅), but will be back to try the other flavors (in bowl form) at some point. I may add a star if the oreo one fulfills my heart's desires.

I ordered the Mint Madness Specialty Milkshake for $20, and I honestly don’t think it was worth it at all. The toppings were not nearly as generous as I expected: just whipped cream, one brownie piece, a scoop of cookie dough, one piece of Oreo, and some chocolate chips at the bottom of the shake. They didn’t even blend the chocolate chips into the milkshake — they just poured them straight in from the package, so they wouldn’t come up through the straw. You can also tell the ingredients are pretty average. The chocolate lacked that rich cocoa-butter aroma, and the whipped cream wasn’t good either.

I also ordered the Triple Chocolate milkshake, which was $10. The chocolate flavor was not rich at all, and it didn’t even have a nice milky taste. Compared with Shake Shack, it’s nowhere close. On top of that, the prices are really expensive. Other than looking good visually, it has no real strengths. I wouldn’t recommend it, and I definitely won’t be coming back.

top_reviews.content: Very cute out of the the way park. Play structures for older and younger kids. Bathrooms are super clean and there’s a nice water fountain. There’s two picnic table and trash, compost, and recycling receptacles.
What a cute little neighborhood park with a beautiful view. I really like the play structure, and there's a bathroom here. The freeway is loud, but if you look around, there's a lot of nature around.

This park is new. It officially opened on March 2, 2018. It has turned an awkwardly shaped and sloped piece of land into a nice neighborhood amenity.

At the time I write this review (March 3, 2018), a fair amount of the park is still fenced off to allow the initial groundcover to take hold.

The biggest attraction will, I think, be the playground structures. There are two sets, 1 fenced and designed for kids under 5, the other unfenced and designed for ages 5-12 (per the signs posted).

I doubt Peggy Thompson Pierce Street Park will become a significant destination for people who don't live within walking distance for the following reasons:
1) It's just too close to the freeway. The freeway dominates all views and contributes significant noise. There is no way that anyone might call this park "peaceful" unless a major accident has stopped all freeway traffic!
2) Unless you have a handicapped placard, parking is on-street in an area that had nearly full on-street parking before the park was built. In other words, I don't recommend driving here!

With that said, I think there are three groups of people who will see this park as a great addition:
1) Families with young kids who live within walking distance
2) Bicyclists using Pierce Street (for whatever reason) as it provides a place to stop and rest a bit
3) Anyone who is nearby and needs to find a public restroom!

google.description: Built in 1869, this Italianate mansion houses a museum with period furnishings & decor.

top_reviews.content:
The Pardee Home Museum (Italianate architecture) was built by the Pardee family.  Three generations lived lived there from 1868 to 1981.  The last survivor put the home in a trust that is run by a Board of Trustees.  It's self-supporting and run by volunteers.  The father (made money in the mines, was an eye doctor and a California State Senator) and his son was Governor of California who made the poppy flower CA's state flower; reformed prisons;  and established the EBMUD.  All furnishings and collections are original and left intact.  The tour is about 1.5 hours. Tour was educational and interesting - it covers the entire residence of 3 floors.  The tour guide was nice and knowledgeable.  She kept the tour intense so you wanted to know more.  She gave insights and tibits of the family.  All questions were answered.

The afternoon tea is delightful.  The food is prepared from scratch with lots of love from the volunteers.  They were friendly, personable and thoughtful.  Since it was the day before Easter, they put some Easter bunny theme to the tea.  Just lovely people who made a delcious three course of food assortment.

I definitely recommend the tour to learn about Oakland history and to visit one of the last standing historical mansions.  Tea was authentic - no crust on the bread :)

Parse Family Museum was like a time capsule with incredible detailing and collections inside. Our work group was able to secure a private garden afternoon tea with 3 courses of goodies and all the english breakfast tea you could ask for. The women there were lovely and patient with us and even gave us each a thank you gift to take home. Following the tea and treats we took the tour which lasted a little over an hour sharing the homes history across 3 floors of unique treasures and facts. There is plenty parking both free and paid on both ends of the street just not directly out front. The ease of access as you come across the overpass made it all the better to get too! Definitely a place I will return to with family.

TL; DR: Great place to experience a tea party (by group reservation only). Interesting Victorian home museum in which to learn about local history, including that it was home to the first fulltime CA governor. House is chilly in cold months so wear layers, but the dinning room has a space heater during tea. Don't forget to bring cash for the donation box, it'd be appreciated :)
---
I visited here with a group for tea service. The entire thing from the set up, baking, and serving was beautifully orchestrated by friendly museum volunteers who delighted us with a lovely spread of tasty tea and baked goods in the historic home's dinning room.

Tea parties are the home museum's main source of income and a great place to celebrate special occasions or just have an outing with a group of friends. The service is hosted by reservation for groups only. There's a minimum number of attendees required. In the winter the max number of tea guests per party is limited to 12 (the size of the dinning room table). In warm weather, the max is closer to 40 people and its hosted in the patio. Check their website for info.

Our visit was concluded with a docent led tour of the house covering the story of the 3 generations of Pardees who lived there. The family was influential in politics, and was also active in medicine. The house is filled with thousands of family artifacts and collections, including some artwork by the talented Mrs. Pardee. There's definitely plenty to see and learn here.

For the sake of time, our tour didn't include a view of the room with old toys and human specimens (remember that least one Pardee was a physician). If you're curious, you could request a view from the docent. I actually was not aware of this room at all until a fellow tour goer asked about it.

Prior to the development of the 'Claremont Court' subdivision, a spring at the top of the Garber St. hill flowed down and created a pond here.  It is said that in the summer, local farmers would bring their cattle to wallow in the cool waters.  The famed painter William Keith is said to have painted the pastoral scene.

With the initial mapping of the subdivision in 1906, a water company took over the spring, and a culvert was built, allowing the creation of the park.   It is reputed to be one of the first suburban residential subdivisions in the US.  The subdivision's development took place during the rapid transition from horses to automobiles.The subdivision initially featured a watering station for horses right in the middle of the gates on Claremont Blvd. The subdivision plan called for (coal) gas street lanterns,  but after the earthquake and fire in San Francisco the idea was discarded.  In some places, the abandoned gas lines can be seen in the parking strips.   The developer was also concerned that automobile parking would detract from sales so prohibitions on the number and location on the lot where cars could be parked were instituted.  A frustrated wealthy car collector built a 'spite house' on Forest Ave. just outside of the subdivision gates that features a large round-table on the first floor with chauffeur lodging above.

Sometime in the 1920's a Monkey tree was planted on the park.  Over the decades it grew to be very large.  During the 1960's, neighborhood children would meet at the tree in the evening to play tag and hide & seek.  The tree was 'base' for the games and eventually a large smooth spot developed on the tree from so many small hands clinging to it's safety.     Eventually, the Monkey tree grew so large that the City decided it was a potential hazard and removed it, but the name remained.

Although many believe it to be a 'dog park', it is not.  The park is reserved for cats on Tuesday and Thursday.

Great local gathering space for kids, dogs, neighbors.  Don't known where the name came from as I have visited the park for decade's & have never seen a monkey.  A permanent picnic table would be a nice addition.

top_reviews.content:
Tried the Afternoon Tea at Nudi Blue.
Beautiful presentation served in a glass case, everything felt like a little piece of art.

Currently, afternoon tea is the primary offering at Nudi Blue. It includes a sweet course, a salad palate cleanser, a savory course, and two tea selections. You can purchase their impressive selection of teas and pastries à la carte, too.

The first course was a delightful selection of five pastries. The majority were croissant dough-based, but in different shapes and portion sizes. The guava croissant burst with tropical flavor, and its laminated layers had a good bounce. Pink guava cream decorated the top and filled the pastry.

I quite liked the Earl Grey NY Roll, which was a slice of croissant topped with earl grey cream. I do wish the candied tea leaves had a stronger flavor, but they looked lovely.

My favorite item was the half-moon croissant. The whipped dill cream cheese held its piped shape well. Artful bits of onion flakes and caviar were sprinkled and dolloped on top. That lovely cucumber ribbon and the dill fronds added nice flavor to each bite. I love all those flavors together, but I should note that I may also have loved the half-moon most because it was the most sizable item.

Both of the tartlets—pear and apple with lychee cream and a seasonal combination of citruses—were quite enjoyable, though messy to eat in a couple bites.

After I ate all my crumbs, I was happy to have a small, palate-cleansing salad served next. The vinaigrette was light and satisfying, and the simple mixed greens were boosted by thin shavings of strawberry, rhubarb, and leek.

And then it was time for the savory course, served on a fun glass case containing an artificial terrarium that evoked a creekside walk. I was less enchanted with this course overall. Honestly, I think that’s mostly because the milk bread used for the two sandwiches tasted stale and dry. The bread was toasted for the vibrantly arrayed smoked duck breast and blueberry sandwich, so that dryness was likely intentional. But as the duck itself was also on the dry side, it didn’t work for me. Also, I’m not a fan of blueberry and that is completely not Nudi Blue’s fault. I wanted to try that sandwich regardless, because it looked so inventive.

The cucumber sandwich included herbal cream cheese, a cucumber gelée, and a rauram leaf on top. Its milk bread was untoasted but still tasted dry and stale to me. It was also bigger than it needed to be? That’s odd to say for a tea sandwich, I know. Following my dining companion’s example, I found it more approachable to eat one layer at a time. It felt like too much cream cheese when taking a full bite. I couldn’t help but compare it with the half-moon croissant from the first course, and it didn’t wow like that one did.

The ham and quinta cheese bite, served on puff pastry, was a pleasant option. It went down fast, and I especially enjoyed the pomegranate seeds that added a burst of acidity to contrast with the richness of ham and cheese.

Much like the tartlets, I enjoyed both scones. The orange and jelly-topped scone had bold flavors but did not linger in my memory like the wagyu scone did. The latter wasn’t visually pleasing with just a slice of quinta cheese melted on top. And I was surprised by how few bits of ground wagyu were in the dough. As with Tanzies, I was made to feel like I was a guest in their house, the service was so warm and welcoming. Will be back soon...

Had a fantastic time here! The outdoor cinema is in a gated area of the former transbay terminal. They've set up a 16'x9' LED screen above a half-sized container with bean bag and lounge chair seating for about 100. I loved the individual headphones, so the sound is excellent and you can't hear the nearby traffic. And you can't beat the view.

I ended up here on a clear, not super windy night. They do offer blankets, but its San Francisco, come prepared! The lounge chairs were surprisingly comfy even for a two hour movie.

They have a limited bar and popcorn/snack bar. There is a full bar in a container outside the theater.

My only minor complaint is that the screen is a little small if you are in the back, but still totally watchable. Will definitely be back!

Great concept, well thought out: the big screen with awesome resolution, the chairs, the blankets, the noise-cancelling headphones. All good. Unfortunately during our show, there was a DJ playing at the outdoor open area and the music was too distracting for us to enjoy the movie. We left half way through as we couldn’t concentrate on the movie.

The headphones provide great audio quality. I'm a little short for the chair and my feet didn't quite touch the floor. Because it is reclined I could not scoot forward to plant my feet to get out of the seat. I asked my friend to help me up and it was still a challenge. The chair collapsed when I got up. Awkward! But otherwise I loved the blanket, the popcorn, and the movie experience.

address: 600 Bellevue Ave, Oakland, CA 94610, United States

google.name: Rotary Nature Center
google.address: 600 Bellevue Ave, Oakland, CA 94610, United States

top_reviews.content:
The grand re-opening was Saturday, Sunday, January 17, 18, 2026. Nicely done, we spent 1.5 hours with both 1st and 4th graders engaged in art or exploring exhibits and preschool play area.

This is not open every day so check official web site for times open.

There is excellent information on various aspects of Lake Merritt, as the oldest bird refuge in the U.S.

Most exhibits are "no touch" but items are not inside cases, so keep your kids close and read signs. One rock exhibit invites touch, but sign is flat on high shelf, so not noticeable. The rest of open display cases have signs saying "do not touch" but visually and informationally are very well done.  I imagine this may change, if public does not take care of exhibits, will try to update review next time we visit.

The 1st grader loved the egg comparison display, of eggs from humming bird, up to osterich size. She was drawing eggs and comparing them, or using art supplies on table to color or add details. The burrowing owl exhibit was my favorite.

The various stuffed birds along the top display shelves, representing the Lake Merritt bird population, had a corresponding identity list.  Lots of people stopped to compare and find the birds on display.

They have a baby/preschool program open to public twice a week,at specific times, with a $5.00 supply fee that looks inviting and a great bargain for parents who loves interactive activities to do WITH your little one.

I remember this center from my children and grand children visiting decades ago, it has been updated and refreshed, especially the preschool are which is inviting and well stocked. We peeked in the cloth boxes on the shelves with various toys. Our favorite was the table with chairs, and in the center was built in box of bones & shells to touch, hold, view in the built-in magnifying glasses in table.

My son remembered it as "Tired". It is nicely refreshed and relevant to today's world.

Incredibly poor management of the Bird Yard by Lake Merritt. No fresh water for the migratory birds. There are literally signs posted saying they need the fresh water and Rotary Nature center hasn't done anything to fix the problem.

I reached out to them several times and offered to help and volunteer and never received a response.

People are not doing their jobs we pay out of our taxes for them to do.

It’s really sad how they let things go over the years. There basically is no sanctuary left. All the plants and water have dried up and died. You can tell that they’re not using fountains or sprinklers to keep the sanctuary going, resulting in all the wild life to disappear.  Homeless camps and garbage surround the sides of the center and the center itself isn’t even open for the public to view its mini museum or to buy bird seeds. Not to mention the water levels of lake Merritt have gone down significantly and the islands located on the lake where some birds reside are dried up and dead. It’s a shame with how expensive it is to live in that area that no money is going into the upkeep of that historical area. Shame on Oakland, and shame on its previous and recent mayors for allowing it to get to that point. There’s plenty of money to keep building luxury apartments that no one can afford to live in though.

The Rotary Nature Center is an awesome place to take little kids. It's small and a little rough around the edges, but kids could care less. There's a live snake and tarantula. They also have bees and others stuffed creatures.

They also have different nature programs, some restricted to those 18+, and volunteer opportunities.

The best place to watch the birds in the nature preserve is right next door. The center sells bird food for a dollar.
Very nice to learn about animals and nature

top_reviews.content: Our daughter and her fiancé had their wedding welcome party at Hammerling Wines a few weeks ago for about 100 guests and it was absolutely perfect. I had friends regretting they'd already chosen a different spot for their upcoming wedding. The space is casual, inviting, and spacious, and the service is friendly, generous, and knowledgeable. And the wines! I drink mostly sparkling, whites, and roses, and Hammerling is my favorite local winery. Highly recommend!

During the event there was never a wait for a glass of wine and the space is lovely we didn't feel like we had to add anything decor wise. I highly recommend this place in general, and especially if considering it for an event! It was perfect!

Being in Celik’s class has not only taught my kid about acting, but also on communicating with others, building confidence on speaking, and learning to be kind and respectful to others. Celik is an experience film maker, director, actor and I feel that he provides a great opportunity for my kid to explore the interest and passion on acting and film making through FABA.

If you are considering taking acting classes and you live anywhere near Berkeley I would suggest contacting Celik and sitting in on a class if you're unsure of which school to attend. top_reviews.content:
A Diorama Museum for the Commons: Public Art on Derby Street
Tucked along Derby Street in Berkeley, you'll find an extraordinary example of art as civic gift—a collection of handcrafted diorama boxes, each a self-contained world visible through small windows. The "Diorama Museum," as one box announces, presents an astonishing range of tableaux: healthy and bleached coral reefs (complete with didactic labels), prehistoric scenes with dinosaurs browsing among ferns, protest vignettes proclaiming "RESIST NOW!", a glittering proclamation of "THEIA'S FATE," folk art compositions with intricate patterns, and even a rendering of Monterey's Cannery Row viewed through a vintage television frame.
What elevates this beyond mere decoration is the deliberate philosophical stance it embodies. These works aren't gated behind museum admission or gallery exclusivity—they exist in the liminal space between private property and public street, offered freely to anyone who walks by. The artist-family (whom I had the privilege of meeting) maintains these pieces for strangers, for neighbors, for the occasional photographer, asking nothing in return. This is art as democratic practice, as radical generosity.
The craftsmanship reveals hours of labor: layered paper constructions, carefully positioned miniatures, painted backdrops, natural materials, found objects transformed. Each diorama invites sustained looking, rewards attention with detail. They speak to environmental concern, political engagement, local history, natural wonder, and pure aesthetic play.
In an era of increasing privatization and digital atomization, these small wooden boxes mounted on posts represent something increasingly rare: art made deliberately, joyfully, for the commons. They remind us that public space can still be a site of encounter, beauty, and shared humanity—if we choose to make it so.
A delightful little public installation, well worth a stop to add some brightness to your day!
